articles.title: A member of one body

claims.t: Everything that reasons shares one reason, as limbs share one body, citizens one city, and every lit place one sun.
claims.shared: Four pictures (body, city, sunlight, soul) with one structure: a single thing present in many, and not split by being shared.

support.quote: As several members in one body united, so are reasonable creatures in a body divided and dispersed
gives: as limbs share one body
Everything that reasons
support.follows: Reasoning beings relate to one another as the parts of one body do.

support.quote: If so, then the world is as it were a city.
gives: citizens one city
support.note: The last step of a chain that starts from reason being common to all.
support.follows: Because reason is common to all, all people are fellow citizens of one city.

support.quote: There is but one light of the sun, though it be intercepted by walls and mountains
gives: every lit place one sun
support.follows: One thing can be present in many places without being divided.

support.quote: So is there but one common intellectual soul, though it seem to be divided.
gives: shares one reason
support.follows: The mind that reasons is one, even though it appears as many minds.

support.quote: of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt them all
gives: shares one reason
Everything that reasons
support.follows: All reasoning beings share a single soul.

claims.changed: Marcus says soul, reason and intellectual soul by turns. The fused claim says “reason” throughout.

claims.t: We are made for one another and for one common work, and that shared life is our own good.
claims.shared: Each says that a reasonable being is directed toward its own kind, whether by its making or by its nature, and two of them call that direction its good.

support.quote: all made and prepared for one common operation
gives: for one common work
We are made
support.follows: Reasoning beings exist to do one shared work.

support.quote: As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and consummation, being a member of it, of a common society
gives: We are made
support.follows: I was made to complete a shared society, as one of its members.

support.quote: Whatsoever therefore is partaker of that reasonable common nature, naturally doth as much and more long after his own kind.
gives: for one another
support.follows: Whatever shares in reason is naturally drawn to others who share in it.

support.quote: Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature.
gives: that shared life is our own good
support.follows: Living with others is what is good for a reasoning being.

support.quote: as doing good to thyself, when thou dost good unto others
gives: our own good
support.note: The good of the other and my own are the same act.
support.follows: When I do good to others, I do good to myself.

claims.t: So each thing I do should aim at the common good, directly or at a distance, and holding to that one aim is what makes me one person.
claims.shared: Two passages draw the same consequence from membership: the aim of action is common. 11.19 adds what the single aim does for the one who holds it.

support.quote: so must every action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that is truly sociable
gives: each thing I do should aim at the common good
support.follows: Every action of mine should help make shared life complete.

support.quote: What action soever of thine therefore that either immediately or afar off, hath not reference to the common good, that is an exorbitant and disorderly action
gives: directly or at a distance
aim at the common good
support.follows: An action with no connection to the common good is out of order, even when the connection would only be distant.

support.quote: so must the end also that we propose unto ourselves, be common and sociable
gives: aim at the common good
support.follows: The goal I set for myself should be a common one.

support.quote: all his actions will be agreeable and uniform; and by that means will be still the same man
gives: holding to that one aim is what makes me one person
support.follows: A person who keeps one goal acts consistently and stays the same person.

claims.t: When I hate someone, wrong them, or resent what happens, I cut myself off, and not from that one thing only but from the whole.
claims.shared: Three pictures of severing (a branch, a limb, a faction). In each the person does it to himself, and in each the cut is from the whole.

support.quote: he that hates and is averse, cuts himself off from his neighbour
gives: When I hate someone
I cut myself off
support.follows: Hatred and aversion are how a person cuts himself off from a neighbour.

support.quote: and knows not that at the same time he divides himself from the whole body, or corporation
gives: from the whole
support.follows: Cutting myself off from one person cuts me off from everyone.

support.quote: such must thou conceive him to make himself, as much as in him lieth, that either is offended with anything that is happened
gives: resent what happens
support.note: The severed hand or foot. 8.32 counts resentment of events as a cut too.
support.follows: Resenting what has happened separates me from the whole, like a severed limb.

support.quote: or that commits anything against the natural law of mutual correspondence, and society among men
gives: wrong them
support.follows: Acting against fellowship separates me in the same way.

support.quote: as one among the people who from such and such a consent and unity, should factiously divide and separate himself
gives: I cut myself off
support.follows: An action that ignores the common good is like breaking away from a united people.

claims.t: Having cut myself off, I can grow back into the whole, because nature is stronger than my leaving.
claims.shared: Two passages say the return is possible in almost the same words. 9.7 gives the reason: reasonable beings cannot finally escape their nature.

support.quote: once cut off we may grow together and become part of the whole again
gives: I can grow back into the whole
support.follows: Someone who has cut himself off can be rejoined.

support.quote: if he would himself, he might return, and grow together again
gives: I can grow back
support.follows: Return is possible if the person wants it.

support.quote: But though they fly from nature, yet are they stopt in their course, and apprehended.
gives: nature is stronger than my leaving
support.follows: Reasoning beings cannot finally escape their nature; it catches up with them.

claims.changed: Both 11.7 and 8.32 credit the return to God. The fused claim credits nature, following 9.7.

single.label: A practice
single.t: I shall often say to myself: I am a member, and not merely a part.
single.quote: use thyself often to say to thyself, I am μέλος, or a member of the mass and body of reasonable substances
single.why: Only 7.10 gives an exercise. It is kept as the article’s practice.
single.follows: I should often tell myself that I am a member of this body.

single.label: A warning
single.t: The more often I cut myself off, the harder the return.
single.quote: But if this happen often the misery is that the further a man is run in this division, the harder he is to be reunited and restored again
single.why: Only 11.7 says the return gets harder. One witness, so it is not fused into claim 5.
single.follows: Each repeated separation makes reunion harder.

decisions: Reads body, city, sunlight and soul as four pictures of one claim. Marcus never lines them up himself.
Draws claim 5 from claim 1. Marcus states the return and does not derive it.
Says “nature” where two of the three passages behind claim 5 say God.
articles.limit: Nine of the ten passages feed the article. That is also a risk: fusing smooths over differences. 4.4 argues for the unity step by step, and 9.7 argues from the elements; the article states the unity and keeps neither argument.

aside.8.52: A wish to share one mind as we share one air. Close to claim 1, but a wish and not a statement.

statement.t: I am a member of one body of reasoning beings, made for a shared life with them.

parts.words: made for a shared life with them

statement.kind: Many pictures, one claim; then its consequences
statement.form: The statement gathers claims 1 and 2. Each of those is fused from four passages that use different pictures: body, city, sunlight, soul. The other subarticles are what Marcus draws from it.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section considers that reasoning beings might not be one. The doubt is taken up under Article 3.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the two central claims gain a second author, the body picture gains an arch beside it, and the article gains a concrete act and a second exercise. One claim is qualified: Seneca allows me to withdraw from the crowd.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement gains the arch: we do not only belong together, we hold one another up.

items.quote: All this that you see, in which things divine and human are enclosed, is one
gives: as limbs share one body
items.follows: Everything there is, divine and human, is one.
items.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people; “All this that you see” is the universe, things divine and human together, of which we are parts.

items.quote: Nature brought us forth as kin, since she begot us from the same things and for the same things. She planted in us love for one another and made us fit for fellowship.
gives: We are made
for one another
items.follows: Nature made us kin, from the same things and for the same things, and gave us love for one another.
items.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “Us” is all human beings; “she” is Nature.

items.quote: no one can live happily who looks only at himself, who turns everything to his own advantage: you must live for another, if you want to live for yourself
gives: that shared life is our own good
items.follows: No one lives happily for himself alone; to live for myself I have to live for another.
items.context: Opens on friendship (a friend’s interest is mine), then widens to all fellow men in 48.3. “Another” is any other person, the friend first.

items.label: why
items.t: We hold one another up as the stones of an arch do: without that support the arch falls.
items.why: Marcus has body, city, sunlight and soul. The arch adds something none of them states: that each part depends on the others to stand at all.

support.quote: Our fellowship is very like an arch of stones, which would fall if the stones did not block one another, and is held up by that very thing
support.follows: Human fellowship stands the way an arch of stones does: only because its parts hold one another up.
support.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “Our fellowship” is human fellowship as a whole, not one friendship.

items.label: action
items.t: So my hands should be ready for anyone who needs help.
items.why: Marcus’s claim says to aim at the common good. Seneca names what that looks like when someone is in front of me.

support.quote: by her command let our hands be ready for those who need help
support.follows: By Nature’s command we should be ready to help those who need help.
support.context: The practical close of Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people. “Her” is Nature; those to be helped are people in need, like the shipwrecked and the starving just named.

items.label: practice
items.t: I shall keep one line in my heart and on my lips: I am human, and nothing human is foreign to me.
items.why: A second exercise beside Marcus’s own. The line is from the playwright Terence; Seneca quotes it as something to repeat.

support.quote: Let that verse be both in the heart and on the lips: “I am human: I count nothing human foreign to me.”
support.follows: I should keep ready a line that says nothing human is foreign to me.
support.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “That verse” is a line of Terence, unnamed here, that Lucilius is told to keep ready.

items.t: Seneca draws a line Marcus does not. He agrees that I must not hate the many, but he tells me to withdraw from the crowd as far as I can and to choose the company that makes me better. For Marcus, turning away from anyone is the start of cutting myself off.

support.quote: do not become like the bad because they are many
support.follows: I should not become like bad people because there are many of them.
support.context: Letter 7, on crowds: “the bad” are the crowd met in public. Seneca has said one must either imitate it or hate it, and here rejects imitating it.

amend.t: , each of us holding the others up as the stones of an arch do
— though stepping back from the crowd to keep better company is not cutting myself off

articles.title: The work that belongs to me

claims.t: Among other people, I mean well by my own kind and aim at the common good. This comes first.
claims.shared: All three lists have this item, and two of them put it first.

support.quote: That therefore which is chief in every man's constitution, is, that he intend the common good.
gives: aim at the common good
support.follows: The most important thing in a human being is to aim at the common good.

support.quote: first, to be kindly affected towards them that are of the same kind and nature as he is himself
gives: mean well by my own kind
support.follows: The first thing proper to a human being is goodwill toward other human beings.

support.quote: when in all its motions and resolutions it takes its level at the common good only
gives: aim at the common good
support.follows: A reasoning nature does well when all its impulses aim only at the common good.

support.quote: as we are bound to do them good, and to bear with them
gives: mean well by my own kind
support.follows: We are bound to do good to other people and to be patient with them.

claims.t: With my body, I do not let its urges rule me. Reason was made to be in charge of the body.
claims.shared: Two of the three lists have this item. 8.6 has none about the body; it speaks of desire in general.

support.quote: The second is, that he yield not to any lusts and motions of the flesh.
gives: I do not let its urges rule me
support.follows: A human being should not give in to bodily urges.

support.quote: to contemn all sensual motions and appetites
gives: I do not let its urges rule me
support.follows: It is proper to a human being to look down on bodily urges and appetites.

support.quote: For by nature she was ordained to command all in the body.
gives: Reason was made to be in charge of the body
support.follows: Reason is by nature the part that commands the body.

support.quote: But one whereby pleasure and voluptuousness may be resisted and opposed, I see: continence.
support.note: Names the virtue that does this work.
support.follows: Self-restraint is the virtue that resists pleasure.
gives: I do not let its urges rule me

claims.t: In my judgments I take care: I do not accept what is false or uncertain, and I do not judge in a hurry.
claims.shared: All three lists have this item. 8.6 puts it first and 7.30 last.

support.quote: The third thing proper to man by his constitution, is, to avoid all rashness and precipitancy; and not to be subject to error.
gives: I do not judge in a hurry
I do not accept what is false or uncertain
support.follows: A human being should avoid haste in judging and should not be deceived.

support.quote: in matter of fancies and imaginations, it gives no consent to that which is either false uncertain
gives: I do not accept what is false or uncertain
support.follows: A reasoning nature does well when it does not agree to anything false or uncertain.

support.quote: to discern rightly all plausible fancies and imaginations
gives: I take care
support.follows: It is proper to a human being to judge persuasive impressions correctly.

support.quote: or be apt to be deceived, or rash, and inconstant
gives: I do not judge in a hurry
I do not accept what is false or uncertain
support.note: Said of what destroys justice: being deceived, rash or inconstant.
support.follows: Being deceived, hasty or changeable makes justice impossible.

claims.t: Doing this work is living according to my own nature. That is why it cannot harm me, and why doing it makes me content.
claims.shared: Joy, content, happiness and “not hurtful” are four words in four passages for one claim: proper work is its own good.

support.quote: The true joy of a man, is to do that which properly belongs unto a man.
gives: doing it makes me content
support.follows: A human being’s real joy is in doing what belongs to a human being.

support.quote: Every particular nature hath content, when in its own proper course it speeds.
gives: living according to my own nature
support.follows: Every nature is content when it proceeds along its own course.

support.quote: So a man as long as he doth that which is proper unto a man, his labour cannot be against nature
gives: living according to my own nature
support.follows: Work that is proper to a human being cannot be against nature.

support.quote: and if it be not against nature, then neither is it hurtful unto him
gives: it cannot harm me
support.follows: What is not against nature does not harm the one who does it.

support.quote: and she hath her end, and by consequent her happiness
gives: doing it makes me content
support.follows: A mind that keeps to these things reaches its goal, and so is happy.

support.quote: To a reasonable creature, the same action is both according to nature, and according to reason.
support.note: Why work done by reason counts as natural.
support.follows: For a reasoning being, acting by reason and acting by nature are the same.

claims.t: The work is the act itself, not its result and not what I feel. And when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action.
claims.shared: Two passages place the good in the act itself. Three more, in three images, say an obstacle is turned into the next object of action.

support.quote: The final ends and consummations of actions are nothing at all to a man's nature.
gives: not its result
support.follows: How an action finally turns out is not part of what a human being is.

support.quote: so neither doth the true good or evil of a reasonable charitable man consist in passion, but in operation and action
gives: The work is the act itself, not its result and not what I feel
support.follows: A person’s good and bad lie in what he does, not in what he feels.

support.quote: For by these the mind doth turn and convert any impediment whatsoever, to be her aim and purpose.
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
support.follows: The mind can turn any obstacle into its new aim.

support.quote: so that whatsoever it is that falls out contrary to its first intentions, even that afterwards it makes its proper object
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
support.follows: When something goes against its first plan, the mind takes that very thing as its next object.

support.quote: it may use them as fit and proper objects, to the furtherance of whatsoever it intended
gives: dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
support.follows: A reasoning being can use any obstacle to further what it set out to do.

single.label: Only in one list
single.t: I may add a fourth work: to contemplate the nature of the universe.
single.quote: to contemplate the nature of the universe
single.why: Neither of the other two lists has it, so it is not fused. Article 4 takes it up.
single.follows: Contemplating the nature of the universe is also proper to a human being.

single.label: Only in one list
single.t: And I may welcome gladly whatever the common nature deals out.
single.quote: when it willingly and gladly embraceth, whatsoever is dealt and appointed unto it by the common nature
single.why: Only 8.6 puts this in the list. It is the whole subject of Article 3.
single.follows: A reasoning nature does well when it gladly accepts what nature assigns it.

single.label: A direction
single.t: To these I shall apply my mind and go straight on, without distraction about other things.
single.quote: To these things then, let the mind apply herself and go straight on, without any distraction about other things
single.why: Only 7.30 turns the list into an instruction.
single.follows: The mind should keep to these three things and not be distracted by others.

decisions: Treats the three lists as versions of one list. Marcus never says they are the same list.
Names the three places “other people, my body, my judgments”, and sums them up as “letting reason lead”. The names and the summary are the editor’s.
Joins the passages about outcomes with those about obstacles in claim 5, as two sides of one point.
articles.limit: The alignment is clean for two of the three items. The item about the body is missing from 8.6, and each list has something the others lack. Those leftovers are shown under “said once”.

aside.11.18: The elements keep their place; the mind that resents does not. An argument for submission, nearer to Article 3.
aside.9.1: A long passage that calls injustice, lying and pleasure-seeking impious. It argues for the same three works from piety, a ground the article does not use.
aside.7.42: What offers nothing to reason or to charity is beneath the reasonable faculty. A test for objects, not a description of the work.

statement.t: My work is to let reason lead in how I treat other people, in how I handle my body, and in how I judge.
statement.form: Three passages (7.30, 8.25 and 8.6) each list what is proper to a human being, in different words and at different lengths. The statement and the three claims under “In action” come from aligning those lists item by item.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what remains if reason is not what a human being is for.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author and Practice gains a way to keep to the work on a crowded day. One claim is qualified: Seneca is milder about the body.
seneca.statement: The statement stands. Seneca gives the same reason for it: reason is what belongs to a human being alone.

items.quote: It is mine, as the one who is praised: because nature bore me as someone who loves all people, I both rejoice to have done good and am glad to have found grateful interpreters of the virtues.
gives: mean well by my own kind
items.follows: Being praised by good people is my own good as the one praised: since nature made me someone who loves all people, I rejoice to have done good and am glad to have found people who are grateful for it.
items.context: Letter 102: renown is praise given to a good man by good men. Asked whose good it is, the one praised or the ones praising, Seneca answers: both.

items.quote: I admit that holding our own body dear is planted in us; I admit that we act as its guardians.
gives: I do not let its urges rule me
items.follows: It is planted in us to hold our bodies dear, and we hold them in our guardianship.
items.context: Letter 14, on withdrawing from the world. Seneca grants that we hold our bodies dear, then says we must not be their slaves; “our guardianship” is our charge of the body.

items.quote: Never will this flesh drive me to fear, never to a pretence unworthy of a good man
gives: Reason was made to be in charge of the body
items.follows: Seneca will never let his body drive him into fear or into a pretence unworthy of a good man.
items.context: Letter 65: Seneca calls his body a chain on his freedom. “This flesh” is his body, and the pretence is one he might put on to protect it.

items.quote: And what is it that this reason demands of him? A very easy thing: to live according to his own nature
gives: living according to my own nature
items.follows: What reason asks of a human being is to live by his own nature.
items.context: Seneca has just said a man’s own good is reason perfected in the soul; “his own nature” is the nature of man as a reasoning animal.

items.quote: What is peculiar to a human being? Reason
gives: doing it makes me content
items.follows: What belongs to a human being alone is reason.
items.context: The same proof that the honourable is the only good. “Peculiar to a human being” means what a human being has and animals and plants do not.

items.quote: Why would I not seek them? Not because they are goods, but because they are according to nature
gives: The work is the act itself, not its result
items.follows: Health, rest and freedom from pain may be sought because they are according to nature, not because they are goods.
items.context: Letter 92, on the happy life. An objector asks whether health, rest and freedom from pain, which do not hinder virtue, should be sought; “them” are those three.

items.label: practice
items.t: On a crowded day I lend myself to my affairs; I do not hand myself over to them.
items.why: Marcus says to keep to the three things and not be distracted. Seneca says how that is done when business cannot be avoided.

support.quote: For I do not hand myself over to affairs but lend myself to them
support.follows: Seneca lends himself to his affairs and does not give himself up to them.
support.context: Opening of Letter 62: people pretend that many affairs block their studies. Seneca says of himself that he has time and that wherever he is he is his own.

items.t: Seneca is milder than Marcus here. The body is ours to look after, and it may be given something; it is only not to be obeyed. Marcus’s passages speak of despising its urges. Seneca is not consistent: in Letter 65.22 he too calls despising the body freedom.

support.quote: I do not deny that it should be indulged
support.follows: The body may be allowed some indulgence.
support.context: Fixture sentence: what the passage around this quote is about.

amend.t: — which does not mean despising the body: it is mine to look after, and may be given something

articles.title: What happens to me

claims.role: It comes from one chain of causes
claims.t: What happens to me is not a random blow from outside. It comes from the same chain of causes that produced me.
claims.shared: Five passages use the same family of words: connection, concatenation, coherence, linked, correspondence. Each says events hold together and reach me through that holding.

support.quote: For by the same coherence of causes, by which thy substance from all eternity was appointed to be, was also whatsoever should happen unto it, destinated and appointed.
gives: It comes from the same chain of causes that produced me
support.follows: The causes that produced me also produced everything that happens to me.

support.quote: from the very beginning by the series and connection of the first causes, it hath ever had a reference unto thee
gives: It comes from the same chain of causes
support.follows: What happens to me was connected to me from the beginning through the chain of causes.

support.quote: All things are linked and knitted together, and the knot is sacred
gives: chain of causes
support.follows: Everything is connected to everything else.

support.quote: that first and general connection, and concatenation of all those things
gives: chain of causes
support.follows: Even what is called chance depends on one connected order.

support.quote: not a bare succession, but an admirable correspondence and affinity
gives: not a random blow from outside
support.follows: Events do not merely follow one another; they fit together.

claims.t: It serves the whole of which I am a part, and what serves the whole is not bad for the part.
claims.shared: Four passages say what happens is useful to the whole. Two of them add the step to the part.

support.quote: Whatsoever in any kind doth happen to any one, is expedient to the whole.
gives: It serves the whole
support.follows: What happens to any individual is useful to the whole.

support.quote: For this whatsoever it be, should not have been produced, had it not conduced to the good of the universe.
gives: It serves the whole
support.follows: Nothing would have happened unless it helped the good of the universe.

support.quote: is both necessary, and conducing to the whole (part of which thou art)
gives: the whole of which I am a part
support.follows: What happens is necessary and helps the whole, and I am part of that whole.

support.quote: must of necessity for every particular nature, be good and behoveful
gives: what serves the whole is not bad for the part
support.follows: What preserves the whole is good for each part.

support.quote: it is against reason that a part should complain of anything that happens for the good of the whole
gives: what serves the whole is not bad for the part
support.follows: A part has no reason to complain of what happens for the good of the whole.

claims.t: So I shall accept it, and more than accept it: fit myself to it and be glad of it, as I take a harsh prescription for the sake of health.
claims.shared: Four passages give the same instruction with rising warmth: accept, fit yourself, embrace, be pleased. Only 5.8 has the physician.

support.quote: These therefore let us accept of in like manner, as we do those that are prescribed unto us our physicians.
gives: as I take a harsh prescription for the sake of health
So I shall accept it
support.follows: I should accept what happens as I accept a doctor’s prescription.

support.quote: Accept then, and be pleased with whatsoever doth happen, though otherwise harsh and un-pleasing
gives: be glad of it
So I shall accept it
support.follows: I should accept what happens and be glad of it, even when it is harsh.

support.quote: Fit and accommodate thyself to that estate and to those occurrences, which by the destinies have been annexed unto thee
gives: fit myself to it
support.follows: I should adapt myself to the circumstances I have been given.

support.quote: to like and embrace all things that happen and are destinated unto him
gives: be glad of it
support.follows: What marks a good person is welcoming everything that happens to him.

support.quote: I am bound to embrace and accept of
gives: So I shall accept it
support.follows: I am bound to accept what follows from the general order.

claims.t: None of it is unusual. Sickness, death and slander are as ordinary as roses in spring.
claims.shared: Two passages make what happens familiar and recurring.

support.quote: Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature, as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer.
gives: as ordinary as roses in spring
None of it is unusual
support.follows: Everything that happens is as ordinary as the seasons.

support.quote: Of the same nature is sickness and death; slander, and lying in wait
gives: Sickness, death and slander
support.follows: Sickness, death, slander and treachery are ordinary in the same way.

support.quote: Up and down, from one age to another, go the ordinary things of the world; being still the same.
gives: None of it is unusual
support.follows: The same ordinary things recur in every age.

claims.t: And if nothing governs the world, I still have a reason of my own, and can govern what is mine with it.
claims.shared: Four passages end the same way: grant that all is chance, and my own reason remains. This is the most repeated move in the section.

support.quote: or if all things go by chance and fortune, yet mayest thou use thine own providence in those things that concern thee properly; and then art thou well
gives: can govern what is mine with it
support.follows: Even if everything is chance, I can still use my own foresight in what concerns me.

support.quote: thou thyself hast obtained a reasonable faculty, whereby thou mayest govern thine own life and actions
gives: I still have a reason of my own
can govern what is mine with it
support.follows: Even in a world without order, I have reason and can govern my life with it.

support.quote: it is lawful for me to deliberate myself
gives: can govern what is mine with it
support.follows: Even if the gods plan nothing, I may still deliberate about my own affairs.

support.quote: what doest thou trouble thyself for?
support.note: The conclusion Marcus draws on the atomist case.
support.follows: If everything is only atoms, there is nothing for me to be troubled about.

single.label: A warning
single.t: Each time I am displeased with what happens, I cut something away from the whole, as far as lies in me.
single.quote: thou doest (as much as lieth in thee) cut off, and in some sort violently take somewhat away, as often as thou art displeased with anything that happeneth
single.why: One witness in this section. 8.32, in the section behind Article 1, says the same with a severed limb.
single.follows: Being displeased with what happens damages the whole, as far as I am able to damage it.

single.label: An addition
single.t: And I shall love the people fate has given me to live with, and love them truly.
single.quote: and love those men whom thy fate it is to live with; but love them truly
single.why: Only 6.35 turns acceptance toward people. It is kept apart for a later article.
single.follows: I should genuinely love the people I happen to live among.

decisions: Presents the section as one argument by cases. Marcus gives the cases in four passages and never the whole chain in one place.
Softens “good for the part” to “not bad for the part”. 1.17 says “good and behoveful”; 9.38 says only that the part has no ground to complain.
Says nothing about acting to change what can be changed. That is Article 2. Accepting what has happened is not an instruction to do nothing.
articles.limit: Claims 1 to 4 hold only in the first case. If you do not think the world is governed, the article reduces to claim 5, and Marcus would not object: he says so himself.

aside.7.22: A list of reminders about order, death, pain and praise. Too many subjects to fuse with anything here.
aside.3.12: Questions to ask of any impression, tracing each thing to God, fate or a neighbour. A practice of examination, nearer to judgment.
aside.4.8: What happens, happens justly. A stronger claim than claim 2, and only this passage makes it.

statement.t: Whatever happens to me, I accept it and do not complain.
statement.kind: An argument by cases, found four times
statement.form: This is an argument by cases, and Marcus makes it four times in this section. “Why” holds the first case, that the world is governed. “If I doubt it” holds the second.

empty.practice: No passage in this section gives an exercise. The physician of 5.8 is a comparison, not something to do.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca this article changes most. Every claim gains a second author, the empty Practice label gets two exercises, “Why” gets a new argument, and “be glad of it” is qualified.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement gains a preparation: I accept what happens, and I think ahead to it.

items.quote: These things are decreed; they are not accidents.
gives: not a random blow from outside
items.follows: Troubles like these are decreed, not accidental.
items.context: Seneca has just listed his own illness, sick slaves and lost income; “These things” are those troubles, which he calls inevitable.

items.quote: the very things by which he seems to be harmed serve to preserve the universe
gives: It serves the whole
items.follows: What seems to harm me serves to preserve the universe.
items.context: Seneca names the inner defence against Fortune: not chafing at what happens. “The very things” are the events that seem to harm us.

items.quote: this is how I have been formed: I do not obey god but agree with him
gives: So I shall accept it
more than accept it
items.follows: Seneca has been formed to agree with God and not to obey him.
items.context: Seneca answers a complaining Lucilius. To “agree with him” is to agree with God about the illness and losses Seneca has just listed as his own, which he says are decreed and are not accidents.

items.quote: Our mind must be fitted to this law; let it follow this, let it obey this; and let it think that whatever happens ought to have happened, and not wish to scold nature.
gives: So I shall accept it
items.follows: My mind should be fitted to nature’s law, think that whatever happens ought to have happened, and not scold nature for it.
items.context: “This law” is nature’s order of changing seasons and opposites, which we cannot alter; “it” is our mind, and “whatever happens” is whatever that order brings.

items.quote: None of these things is unusual, none is unexpected.
gives: None of it is unusual
items.follows: Setbacks like these are neither unusual nor unexpected.
items.context: “These things” are Lucilius’s slaves running away; Seneca widens it at once to every knock on life’s journey.

items.quote: Whether the fates bind us by an inexorable law, or god, the arbiter of the universe, has arranged everything, or chance drives and tosses human affairs about without order, philosophy ought to protect us.
gives: And if nothing governs the world
items.follows: Even if chance drives everything, philosophy is still my protection.
items.context: Seneca answers the objection that philosophy is useless if fate, god or chance rules: in each case we need it. The third case is “chance”.

items.label: why
items.t: And refusing changes nothing: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling.
items.why: Marcus argues from the good of the whole. This argues from the uselessness of refusing. The line is by Cleanthes, in Seneca’s translation.

support.quote: Lead me, O father and ruler of the high heaven, wherever you have decided: there is no delay in obeying; I am here, and eager.
support.follows: The speaker asks Jupiter to lead him wherever Jupiter has decided, and promises to obey without delay.
support.context: Letter 107, on obeying the order of the universe, ends with lines of the Stoic Cleanthes that Seneca has put into Latin. They are spoken to Jupiter.

items.label: practice
items.t: I shall think ahead to everything that can happen, not only to what usually does, so that the blow is lighter when it comes.
items.why: Marcus gives no exercise in this section. Seneca gives this one in three letters.

support.quote: the mind must be sent ahead to everything, and what must be thought of is not whatever usually happens but whatever can happen
support.follows: I should think ahead to what can happen, not only to what usually happens.
gives: think ahead to everything that can happen, not only to what usually does
support.context: Written after fire destroyed Lyons and shook his friend Liberalis; “everything” is whatever Fortune can do, since the unexpected weighs heaviest.

support.quote: When an evil has been thought out beforehand, its blow comes soft.
support.follows: A misfortune I have already thought about hits less hard.
gives: the blow is lighter when it comes
support.context: Follows a picture of the man who hears of chains and exile calmly; “an evil” is any such threatened hardship, new only to the unprepared.

support.quote: Whatever has been long expected is lighter when it comes.
support.follows: What I have long expected is easier when it arrives.
gives: the blow is lighter when it comes
support.context: The closing advice of a letter on illness: keep Fortune’s whole power before your eyes. “Whatever” is any blow she may strike.

items.label: practice
items.t: For a few days at a time I shall live on the plainest food and clothing, and ask myself: is this what I was afraid of?
items.why: A second exercise, done with the body and not only in thought.

support.quote: fit in some days on which, content with the scantiest and cheapest food and with coarse and rough clothing, you say to yourself, “Is this what was feared?”
support.follows: I should spend set days living poorly and ask myself whether this is what I feared.
support.context: A lesson for the Saturnalia: rehearse poverty while Fortune is kind, so that she cannot catch me off guard. The “this” of the question is being poor.

items.label: doubt
items.t: In that case my stance changes too: a god I follow gladly, but chance I only endure, and defy.
items.why: Marcus says only that I can still govern myself. Seneca adds how to stand toward a world run by chance.

support.quote: It will urge us to obey god willingly, and Fortune defiantly; it will teach you to follow god and bear chance.
support.follows: Philosophy teaches me to obey a god willingly, and to bear chance and defy it.
support.context: “It” is philosophy, our protection whether fate, god or chance rules; the sentence sets how to stand toward god against how to stand toward Fortune.

items.t: Seneca does not ask me to be glad of the hardship itself. He would rather be spared it; what he wants, if it comes, is to bear it well. Marcus goes further and says a good person welcomes whatever happens.

support.quote: I would want torture to be far from me; but if it has to be endured, I shall wish to carry myself in it bravely, honourably, with spirit.
support.follows: I may prefer not to be tortured; if it must be endured, what I wish for is to bear it with courage.
support.context: Lucilius asked whether brave endurance of torture is a thing to wish for; Seneca answers that the bravery is to be wished for, not the torture.

amend.t: , and I prepare for it by thinking ahead to everything that can happen
— though I may still wish to be spared it, and want only to bear it well if it comes

articles.title: The reason that governs the whole

claims.t: The world is one thing, ordered throughout, in which each thing helps to cause the others.
claims.shared: Four passages call the world one: one living substance, a κόσμος, a union, “one and general”.

support.quote: Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living substance, and having but one soul
gives: The world is one thing
support.follows: I should always think of the world as one living thing with one soul.

support.quote: and how all things that are, concur in the cause of one another's being
gives: each thing helps to cause the others
support.follows: Everything that exists helps cause everything else.

support.quote: Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all disposed and governed by certain order
gives: ordered throughout
support.follows: The world is an ordered whole.

support.quote: or it is an union consisting of order, and administered by Providence
gives: ordered throughout
support.note: The second of two cases. The first is under “said once”.
support.follows: The world is a unity, ordered and governed by providence.

support.quote: can at one time subsist, and coexist in that both one and general, which we call the world
gives: The world is one thing
support.follows: Everything that happens can exist together in one world.

claims.t: What governs it is reason. It has no cause to do evil, it is for community, and even what looks harmful follows from something good.
claims.shared: Four passages describe the governing reason: without evil, for community, caring for reasonable creatures, and producing harm only as a by-product.

support.quote: That rational essence that doth govern it, hath in itself no cause to do evil.
gives: It has no cause to do evil
What governs it is reason
support.follows: The reason that governs the world has no motive to do evil.

support.quote: That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for community and society
gives: it is for community
What governs it is reason
support.follows: The reason that governs the world aims at community.

support.quote: are but (as the thorn and the mire) the necessary consequences of goodly fair things
gives: even what looks harmful follows from something good
support.follows: Harmful things are by-products of good things.

support.quote: they are surely his reasonable and principal creatures, that are the proper object of his particular care and providence
support.note: If it cares for anything in particular, it is for those who reason.
support.follows: If the governing reason cares for anything in particular, it cares for reasoning beings.

claims.role: The same thing rules in me
claims.t: What rules in me is of one kind with it. It moves itself, and it turns everything else in me to its use.
claims.shared: Two passages describe my ruling part in the terms used for the governor of the whole, and 5.18 says outright that they are one kind.

support.quote: So also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful; and is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of.
gives: of one kind with it
support.follows: What is best in me is the same in kind as what governs the world, and deserves the same honour.

support.quote: For it is the very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use, and by whom also thy life is governed.
gives: it turns everything else in me to its use
What rules in me
support.follows: What is best in me uses everything else in me and governs my life.

support.quote: The rational commanding part, as it alone can stir up and turn itself
gives: It moves itself
What rules in me
support.follows: The ruling part of me is the only thing that moves and directs itself.

support.quote: For is it possible that in thee there should be any beauty at all, and that in the whole world there should be nothing but disorder and confusion?
support.note: The likeness used as an argument: from order in me to order in the whole.
support.follows: If there is order in me, there cannot be only disorder in the world.

claims.t: I shall make a habit of asking what causes each thing: the power at work in it, considered apart from its matter, and the one source of all things.
claims.shared: Five passages give the same instruction in the same verbs: consider, behold, contemplate. Each time the object is the cause and not the thing.

support.quote: and not the things themselves only, but the power also by which they are effected
gives: the power at work
what causes each thing
support.follows: I should look at the power that produces things, and not only at the things.

support.quote: Behold it by itself bare and naked, separated from all that is material.
gives: considered apart from its matter
support.follows: I should consider a cause by itself, apart from the material it works on.

support.quote: but consider in thy mind the true fountain of all
gives: the one source of all
support.follows: I should keep in mind the one source that everything comes from.

support.quote: and by what manner of connection and concatenation all things happen
gives: what causes each thing
support.follows: I should think about how everything is connected in its happening.

support.quote: This often thought upon, will much conduce to thy tranquillity.
gives: I shall make a habit
support.follows: Thinking about this often brings calm.

single.label: An instruction
single.t: I shall honour what is chief and most powerful in the world, and in the same way what is chief in myself.
single.quote: Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things.
single.why: Only 5.18 says “honour”. It is the one place where the likeness becomes an instruction.
single.follows: I should honour what is most powerful in the world, which uses and governs everything.

single.label: A strong claim
single.t: Nothing can be hurt by it.
single.quote: neither can anything be hurt by it
single.why: Only 6.1 goes this far. It is kept apart so that claim 2 does not rest on it.
single.follows: Nothing can be harmed by the reason that governs the world.

single.label: The other case
single.t: If the world were only confusion, why should I wish to stay in it?
single.quote: If the first, why should I desire to continue any longer in this fortuit confusion and commixtion?
single.why: Only here does Marcus say how the ungoverned case would feel. Article 3 carries his calmer answer.
single.follows: If the world were mere confusion, there would be no reason to want to remain in it.

decisions: Reads four descriptions of the world as one claim, and four descriptions of its governor as another.
Makes the likeness between the whole and myself the centre of the article. Only 5.18 states it; 4.22 and 6.7 are read in its light.
Keeps “nothing can be hurt by it” out of the fused claim.
articles.limit: All twelve passages are used. This is a belief about the universe and the least argued of the five. If you do not hold it, Articles 1 and 2 still stand on what human beings share, and Article 3 keeps its last claim.

statement.t: The reason that orders the world and the reason that guides me are the same kind of thing.

parts.words: The reason that orders the world
are the same kind of thing

statement.kind: A likeness between the whole and myself
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 describe the world and claim 3 says the same thing is in me. Only 5.18 states the likeness outright; 4.22 and 6.7 are read in its light.

empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes losing sight of this, or recovering it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, all four claims gain a second author, the empty “When it breaks” gets its first item, and “In action” says how to honour what governs the world. One point is qualified: providence may overlook the individual.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement gains its consequence: to honour the reason that governs the world is to be good.

items.quote: All this that you see, in which things divine and human are enclosed, is one
gives: The world is one thing
items.follows: Everything there is, divine and human, is one.
items.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people; “All this that you see” is the universe, things divine and human together, of which we are parts.

items.quote: that is, god.
gives: What governs it is reason
items.follows: The first cause of everything is reason at work.
items.context: Fixture sentence: what the passage around this quote is about.

items.quote: Anyone who thinks they are unwilling to do harm is mistaken: they are not able to.
gives: It has no cause to do evil
items.follows: The gods are not merely unwilling to do harm; they are unable to.
items.context: On the right idea of the gods, which worship needs; “they” are the gods, whom the next section says preside over the world.

items.quote: What is death? Either an end or a crossing.
gives: What rules in me is of one kind with it
items.follows: Death is one of two things: an end, or a crossing.
items.context: The close of Letter 65, on the first cause: god is to the world as the mind is to the body. Seneca then asks what death is.

items.quote: this reason of ours, which comes from that one, is the same
gives: of one kind with it
items.follows: The reason in us is the same as the divine reason, from which it comes.
items.context: Same opening of the letter; “this reason of ours” is the rational part of the human mind, set beside the divine reason.

items.quote: there must be that from which a thing is made, and then that by which it is made: the second is cause, the first is matter.
gives: considered apart from its matter
items.follows: Every thing has something it is made from, its matter, and something it is made by, its cause.
items.context: Letter 65, on the first cause, sets out the Stoic view that everything comes from cause and matter. Here “a thing” is any thing that is made.

items.quote: all those things your side has listed are not many separate causes, but hang from one, from the one that makes
gives: the one source of all things
items.follows: All causes depend on one cause.
items.context: Seneca rejects Plato’s and Aristotle’s lists of causes; “all those things” are those listed causes, and the “one” is the one that makes, which he has just called reason.

items.label: action
items.t: The way to honour what governs the world is to imitate it: to be good.
items.why: Marcus says to honour what is most powerful in the world. Seneca says what the honouring consists of.

support.quote: Do you want to win the favour of the gods? Be good. Whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough.
support.follows: The way to win the favour of the gods is to be good; whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough.
support.context: Letter 95 turns from rules of ritual to the right idea of the gods, who need no servants and do good by nature. Here “them” means the gods; to imitate them is to be good.

items.label: breaks
items.t: To fail here is to quarrel with the order of the universe, and to want to reform the gods sooner than myself.
items.why: Marcus has no passage in this section on what failing looks like. Seneca describes it.

support.quote: small and ignoble, on the other hand, is the one that struggles against it and thinks ill of the order of the world and would rather correct the gods than itself
support.follows: It is a small spirit that fights fate and thinks ill of the order of the world and would sooner correct the gods than itself.
support.context: Close of a letter on accepting what happens as fate’s law; “the small and ignoble one” is the spirit that fights events instead of handing itself over to fate.

items.t: Seneca allows that the gods, while guarding the human race, sometimes overlook the individual. Marcus’s 7.44 says reasoning beings are the object of particular care, and 6.1 that nothing is harmed by the reason that governs.

support.quote: who watch over the human race, sometimes without concern for individuals
support.follows: The gods guard the human race, though they sometimes do not attend to individuals.
support.context: Letter 95 says how to worship the gods: believe in them and acknowledge their goodness. “Who” refers to the gods, who preside over the world.

amend.t: , and the way to honour it is to be good
— though in guarding all of us it may at times overlook one of us

articles.title: What I was made for

claims.t: Each thing is made for something, and bears its own fruit in its own time.
claims.shared: Two passages state the rule, one as making and one as fruit. A third asks the same question of every act and word.

support.quote: Whatsoever is, was made for something: as a horse, a vine.
gives: Each thing is made for something
support.follows: Everything that exists was made for some purpose.

support.quote: Man, God, the world, every one in their kind, bear some fruits.
gives: bears its own fruit
support.follows: Every kind of thing produces something of its own.

support.quote: All things have their proper time to bear.
gives: in its own time
support.follows: Each thing produces it at its proper time.

support.quote: we must presently see what is the proper use and relation of every one
support.note: Said of purposes and actions, taken one by one.
support.follows: For every action, I should ask what its proper use is.

claims.t: What I am for is not to please myself, but to use my reason and to live well with others. That bears fruit for others and for me.
claims.shared: Three passages say what a reasonable being is for. One rules out pleasure, and two name reason exercised with and for others.

support.quote: What then were then made for? to disport and delight thyself?
gives: not to please myself
support.note: Casaubon’s text reads “were then”. The question is put to the reader.
support.follows: It is absurd to think I was made for my own pleasure.

support.quote: See how even common sense and reason cannot brook it.
gives: not to please myself
support.follows: Ordinary good sense rejects the idea.

support.quote: As for reason, that beareth both common fruit for the use of others; and peculiar, which itself doth enjoy.
gives: bears fruit for others and for me
support.follows: Reason produces something for others and something for itself.

support.quote: is careful to preserve his own, in the continual habit and exercise both of reason and sociableness
gives: to use my reason and to live well with others
support.follows: A person who values reason takes care to keep exercising reason and fellowship.

claims.t: What looks like waste or a flaw has a part in how nature works. Nature throws nothing away, and even her by-products are fitting in their own way.
claims.shared: Two passages look at the same thing, the leftovers of a process, from two sides: 8.48 says nature reuses them, 3.2 says they are pleasing as they are.

support.quote: but the nature of the universe hath no such out-place
gives: Nature throws nothing away
support.follows: Nature has nowhere outside itself to discard anything.

support.quote: whatsoever is within her that seems either corrupted, or old, or unprofitable, she can change it into herself, and of these very things can make new things
gives: has a part in how nature works
support.follows: What seems spoiled or useless, nature turns into something new.

support.quote: whatsoever it is that naturally doth happen to things natural, hath somewhat in itself that is pleasing and delightful
gives: even her by-products are fitting in their own way
support.follows: Whatever happens naturally has something pleasing in it.

support.quote: even among all those things which are but mere accessories and natural appendices as it were, there will scarce appear anything unto him, wherein he will not find matter of pleasure and delight
gives: even her by-products are fitting in their own way
support.follows: To someone who looks closely, even nature’s side effects are a pleasure to see.

single.label: A practice
single.t: If the cucumber is bitter, I set it aside; if brambles are in the way, I go round them; and I do not add: what are such things for in the world?
single.quote: Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way? avoid them.
single.why: Only 8.48 gives the practice. Its second half is the next item.
single.follows: I should simply deal with an unpleasant thing and move on.

single.label: A prohibition
single.t: I do not ask of a bitter thing what it is for.
single.quote: Add not presently speaking unto thyself, What serve these things for in the world?
single.why: Only 8.48 forbids the question. It is what the editor’s join in the thought has to reconcile with 8.17.
single.follows: I should not go on to ask what such things are for.

decisions: Uses 9.8 and 6.13 to answer the question that 8.17 asks and leaves open.
Fuses 8.48 with 3.2, the most central passage of the section, as two views of nature’s leftovers.
Joins 8.17 and 8.48 in the last sentence of the thought. Neither passage mentions the other.
articles.limit: This is the smallest and loosest section: seven passages. Each fused claim rests on two or three passages, against four or five in the other articles, so the induction is thinner here.

aside.11.5: What tragedy and comedy were instituted for. Purpose applied to drama, with nothing for a rule of life.

statement.t: I exist for a purpose, as everything does, and my purpose is not my own amusement.

parts.words: I exist for a purpose, as everything does
my purpose is not my own amusement

statement.kind: A rule, its application to me, and its hardest case
statement.form: A rule, its application to me, and the case that seems to break it. “If I doubt it” answers the objection that some things are plainly useless or flawed.

empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes failing at one’s purpose.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, all three claims gain a second author and the empty “When it breaks” gets its first item. The statement is qualified: the work is not for amusement, but it does bring a joy of its own.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement changes: my purpose is not amusement, but the work brings a stern joy. Marcus says the same in 8.25, which belongs to Article 2.

items.quote: Every thing rests on its own good. What recommends the vine is its fruitfulness and the flavour of its wine; what recommends the stag is speed.
gives: Each thing is made for something
items.follows: Each thing is recommended by the good that is its own, as a vine by its wine and a stag by its speed.
items.context: Letter 76 sets out to prove that there is only one good. Each thing, vine, stag or dog, is rated by that for which it is born.

items.quote: whatever is will not be, yet it will not perish but will be dissolved.
gives: in its own time
items.follows: Everything that exists will come to an end, yet it will not perish: it will be dissolved.
items.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: everything, earth and stars included, is born, grows and is extinguished. Here “whatever is” is every thing in the world.

items.quote: What is peculiar to a human being? Reason
gives: to use my reason
items.follows: What belongs to a human being alone is reason.
items.context: The same proof that the honourable is the only good. “Peculiar to a human being” means what a human being has and animals and plants do not.

items.quote: The one who is of use to many is alive; the one who makes use of himself is alive.
gives: bears fruit for others and for me
items.follows: To be alive is to be of use to many and to make use of oneself.
items.context: The letter attacks living for the belly. “The one” is set against those who obey their appetites, some of whom Seneca has just counted among the dead.

items.quote: that man does not live for himself but, most shameful of all, for his belly, for sleep, for lust
gives: not to please myself
items.follows: A man who hides like that does not live for himself; he lives for his belly, for sleep and for lust.
items.context: “That man” is the man who has hidden from affairs and people out of fear and failed desires. It is not anyone at rest, nor anyone enjoying himself.

items.quote: whatever is will not be, yet it will not perish but will be dissolved.
gives: Nature throws nothing away
items.follows: What ceases to exist is not lost; it returns to its elements.
items.context: Fixture sentence: what the passage around this quote is about.

items.label: breaks
items.t: To fail at this is to hide away and go numb. A person who is of use to no one has died before he is dead.
items.why: Marcus has no passage in this section on what failing looks like. Seneca describes it.

support.quote: those who lie hidden and inert are in their house as they would be in a tomb
support.follows: People who lie hidden and inert are in their house as if in a tomb.
support.context: “Those who lie hidden” are the opposite of the man of use to many: people who withdraw into sloth, in a letter about living for the belly.

items.t: Seneca does not remove joy from the purpose. He says the work brings a joy of its own, and that it is a stern one. Marcus says the same elsewhere (8.25, in Article 2), but not in this section.

support.quote: Believe me, true joy is a stern thing.
support.follows: True joy is serious, not light.
support.context: “True joy” is that of a person who can despise death, face poverty and curb his pleasures. Seneca sets it against laughter and a cheerful face.

amend.t: , though doing the work brings a joy of its own, and a stern one

articles.title: What the whole sends in its season

claims.role: What comes is good, and on time
claims.t: Whatever the whole sends me is good for me, and it comes at the right time: nothing that is in season for the world is too early or too late for me.
claims.shared: Both passages say that what the whole of nature brings me is good for me, and both add the time: 10.21 says it is best when it is sent, 4.19 that nothing in season for the world is out of season for me.
claims.changed: 10.21 says “best”; the claim says “good for me”, which is what 4.19 says. 4.19's address to the world (“O World”) becomes a statement about it.

support.quote: That is best for every one, that the common nature of all doth send unto every one,
gives: Whatever the whole sends me is good for me
support.follows: Whatever the nature of the whole sends to each person is what is best for that person.

support.quote: and then is it best, when she doth send it.
gives: it comes at the right time
support.follows: It is best at the moment it is sent, not earlier and not later.

support.quote: Whatsoever is expedient unto thee, O World, is expedient unto me;
gives: is good for me
support.follows: What is good for the world is good for me.

support.quote: nothing can either be 'unseasonable unto me, or out of date, which unto thee is seasonable.
gives: it comes at the right time
nothing that is in season for the world is too early or too late for me
support.follows: Nothing that comes at the world's right time can come at the wrong time for me.

claims.t: So I want what the world wants. Whatever its seasons bring, I count as a good harvest; and when I pray, I pray for everyone, not for myself alone.
claims.shared: Three passages make what I want follow what the whole wants: 10.22 joins my longing to the world's, 4.19 counts whatever its seasons bring as good fruit, and 5.7 asks for rain on every field, not on one's own.
claims.changed: 5.7 speaks only of how to pray. The claim reads its prayer for all the fields as one more case of wanting what the whole wants.

support.quote: And so (say I) doth the world bear a certain affection of love to whatsoever shall come to pass
gives: what the world wants
support.follows: The world itself welcomes whatever is going to happen.

support.quote: With thine affections shall mine concur, O world. The same (and no other) shall the object of my longing be which is of thine.
gives: I want what the world wants
support.follows: I will want what the world wants, and nothing else.

support.quote: Whatsoever thy seasons bear, shall ever by me be esteemed as happy fruit, and increase.
gives: Whatever its seasons bring, I count as a good harvest
support.follows: I should count whatever the world's seasons bring as a good harvest.

support.quote: O rain, rain, good Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.
gives: I pray for everyone
support.follows: The Athenians asked for rain on all their fields together, not on one man's.

support.quote: Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not every one for himself in particular alone.
gives: when I pray, I pray for everyone, not for myself alone
support.follows: If I pray at all, I should pray simply and for all, not for myself alone.

claims.t: Every part of the world has its own work, as the sun has one task and the rain another; yet the parts are drawn to one another, and all of them work toward one end.
claims.shared: Three passages picture the world as many parts bound into one: 6.38 by separate tasks that serve one end, 4.19 by all things coming from nature and tending back to it, 10.22 by earth and sky longing for each other.
claims.changed: Drops Aesculapius and the stars' particular charges; keeps the sun and the rain.

support.quote: Doth either the sun take upon him to do that which belongs to the rain?
gives: as the sun has one task and the rain another
support.follows: Each power in the world keeps to its own task and does not take over another's.

support.quote: Though they all differ one from another, and have their several charges and functions by themselves, do they not all nevertheless concur and co-operate to one end?
gives: Every part of the world has its own work
all of them work toward one end
support.follows: Different as they are, each with its own task, the stars all work together toward one end.

support.quote: from thee are all things, in thee all things subsist, and to thee all tend.
gives: all of them work toward one end
support.follows: Everything comes from nature, exists in it and tends back to it.

support.quote: The earth, saith the poet, doth often long after the rain. So is the glorious sky often as desirous to fall upon the earth, which argues a mutual kind of love between them.
gives: the parts are drawn to one another
support.follows: Parts of the world are drawn to one another, as the earth and the sky are.

single.label: A practice
single.t: I speak of the world as a citizen speaks of the city he loves: I call it the dear city of God.
single.quote: Could he say of Athens, Thou lovely city of Cecrops; and shalt not thou say of the world, Thou lovely city of God?
single.why: Only 4.19 gives words to say. They are kept as the article's practice.
single.follows: If a man can call Athens a lovely city, I can call the world the lovely city of God.

single.label: Meeting an obstacle
single.t: When something stands in my way, I do not throw myself at it and I do not give way. I hold steady and give light to whatever can take it; what will not take it loses by its own fault.
single.quote: she must not violently, and by way of an impetuous onset light upon them; neither must she fall down; but she must stand, and give light unto that which doth admit of it. For as for that which doth not, it is its own fault and loss, if it bereave itself of her light.
single.why: Only 8.54 says how to meet what resists me. It shows what failing looks like, an attack or a collapse, and the way back.
single.follows: Meeting an obstacle, the mind should neither attack it nor collapse, but hold steady and give light where it is received.

decisions: Reads the world that loves whatever comes to pass (10.22), the world addressed in 4.19 and the common nature of all (10.21) as one whole, and writes “the whole” or “the world” for all three.
Puts 5.7, a prayer for rain on every field, into claim 3 as a case of wanting what the whole wants. 5.7 itself speaks only of how to pray.
Keeps 8.54, the sunbeam, as the article's way back. It is about meeting obstacles, which no other passage of the section mentions.
Leaves out the last sentence of 10.22, a note on a Greek turn of phrase.
articles.limit: Six passages, and 4.19 feeds every claim, so the article leans on it. Claim 1 rests on pictures (sun and rain, stars, earth and sky) rather than on an argument: it shows an order in the whole but does not prove one.

statement.t: What the whole sends me is good for me and comes at the right time, so I want what the world wants.

parts.words: What the whole sends me is good for me
I want what the world wants

statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: the parts of the world each do their own work toward one end. Claim 2 draws what follows for me: what the whole sends is good and timely. Claim 3, and the end of the statement, is the will that follows from that.

inferences.why: Fixture: no passage says “so”; the step from what is sent to what I want is the editor’s.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section considers that what the whole sends might not be good for me. The article states the trust and does not argue for it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, each of the three claims gains a second witness, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: paying for the hard things willingly, an answer if I doubt it, a way of holding my ground, and a test for prayer. He challenges one point: he does not want every good alike.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement takes in the hard things: I want what the world wants, and what hurts I pay willingly, as the tax of being alive.

items.quote: whatever is will not be, yet it will not perish but will be dissolved.
gives: it comes at the right time
items.follows: Everything that exists will come to an end, yet it will not perish: it will be dissolved.
items.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: everything, earth and stars included, is born, grows and is extinguished. Here “whatever is” is every thing in the world.

items.quote: this is how I have been formed: I do not obey god but agree with him
gives: I want what the world wants
items.follows: Seneca has been formed to agree with God and not to obey him.
items.context: Seneca answers a complaining Lucilius. To “agree with him” is to agree with God about the illness and losses Seneca has just listed as his own, which he says are decreed and are not accidents.

items.quote: Nature sends these things off to the same place after unequal spans
gives: all of them work toward one end
items.follows: Nature sends all things, each at its own pace, toward the same goal.
items.context: Fixture sentence: what the passage around this quote is about.

items.label: action
items.t: I pay the hard things willingly. Whatever makes me groan or shrink back is part of the tax of being alive, and I do not hope to escape it.
items.why: In this section Marcus speaks of what comes as fruit and as in season; none of his passages names the hard part of it. Seneca does, and says how to bear it.

support.quote: I shall pay no tax unwillingly.
gives: I pay the hard things willingly
support.follows: Seneca will pay every tax he owes, and none of them unwillingly.
support.context: From Letter 96, where Seneca tells Lucilius to agree with God. The “tax” is not money: the next sentence says that the taxes of life are everything at which we groan or take fright.

support.quote: And all the things at which we groan, at which we take fright, are the taxes of life: from these, my Lucilius, do not hope for exemption and do not ask for it.
gives: Whatever makes me groan or shrink back is part of the tax of being alive
I do not hope to escape it
support.follows: What makes us groan or take fright is one of the taxes of life, and we should neither hope for exemption from it nor ask for it.
support.context: Said to Lucilius, who had feared for his life in an illness. The things that make us groan are the illness, losses, toil and fear listed just before.

items.label: practice
items.t: I ask God only for what I could ask for aloud, and I speak with God as if others were listening.
items.why: 5.7 says to pray for all and not for oneself alone, but gives no test. Seneca gives one: a prayer I could not say aloud is one I should not make.

support.quote: Know that you are released from all desires at the point when you have come to ask god for nothing except what you can ask for openly.
gives: I ask God only for what I could ask for aloud
support.follows: A person is released from his desires once he asks God only for what he could ask for openly.
support.context: Seneca has just told Lucilius to drop his old prayers and ask for a sound mind. The saying is Athenodorus’s; to ask “openly” is to ask only for what others may hear.

support.quote: live with people just as if god saw, speak with god just as if people heard
gives: I speak with God as if others were listening
support.follows: I should live as if God saw me and speak with God as if people heard me.
support.context: Seneca’s own advice, drawn from that saying: people whisper to the gods the shameful prayers they do not want another person to know. To “speak with god” is to pray.

items.label: breaks
items.t: If I give way to a trouble, it beats me. If I hold my ground and push against it, it is forced back.
items.why: 8.54 says not to throw myself at an obstacle and not to collapse. Seneca agrees about not collapsing, but tells me to push back, which is nearer the onset that Marcus forbids.

support.quote: he will be conquered if he gives way, he will conquer if he braces himself against his pain.
gives: If I give way to a trouble, it beats me
support.follows: Whoever gives way to his pain is conquered; whoever braces himself against it conquers.
support.context: A letter on bearing illness and pain, to Lucilius, who is ill; Seneca recalls his own sickness. The “he” is anyone set in the midst of difficulties, bracing himself against his pain.

support.quote: if you stand against it and choose to push back, it will be driven back.
gives: If I hold my ground and push against it, it is forced back
support.follows: What bears down on me is driven back if I stand against it and push back.
support.context: Same passage. The “it” is a collapse that bears down on you: Seneca’s image for pain, which weighs more heavily on the one who draws himself out from under it.

items.label: doubt
items.role: Even if it is a disaster
items.t: Even if what comes is a disaster, a loss or a wrong, it has no more power over my virtue than a cloud has over the sun: it can hide it, but it cannot make it smaller.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what holds if what comes is not good for me. Seneca answers that even then virtue is not made smaller.

support.quote: the things set in the way of virtue take nothing away from it: it is not smaller, but it shines less.
gives: it can hide it, but it cannot make it smaller
support.follows: The things set in virtue’s way take nothing away from it; it only shines less.
support.context: Seneca argues that a good man is happy even under misfortune. What is “set in the way of virtue” stands there as an object stands before the sun, which is no smaller for it.

support.quote: And so disasters and losses and wrongs have the same power against virtue that a mist has against the sun.
gives: Even if what comes is a disaster, a loss or a wrong
it has no more power over my virtue than a cloud has over the sun
support.follows: Disasters, losses and wrongs have no more power against virtue than a mist has against the sun.
support.context: The conclusion of that comparison: a mist hides the sun and takes nothing from it. The “virtue” is the good man’s, which Seneca holds to be his whole good.

items.t: Seneca does not want every good alike. He prays outright for goods such as joy and peace, and for the strength to bear suffering only if the need comes. Marcus counts whatever the seasons bring as good fruit and does not rank it.

support.quote: Some, as our people think, are first goods, such as joy, peace, the safety of one’s country.
support.follows: Some goods, like joy and peace, come first.
support.context: Fixture sentence: what the passage around this quote is about.

support.quote: Some are second goods, shaped in unlucky material, such as endurance of torture and self-control in a serious illness.
support.follows: Bearing suffering well is a good, but of a second kind.
support.context: Fixture sentence: what the passage around this quote is about.

support.quote: The former goods we shall wish for ourselves outright, the latter if it proves necessary.
support.follows: I may pray for the first kind of good outright, and for the second only if I need it.
support.context: Fixture sentence: what the passage around this quote is about.

amend.t: , the hard things too, which I pay willingly as the tax of being alive
— though I ask outright only for goods like joy and peace, and for the strength to bear pain only if the need comes
